title: A Karate Family, an ₹18-Crore Budget, and ₹69 Crore Later — 'Blast' Just Landed on Netflix
excerpt: The Tamil martial arts blockbuster that nobody saw coming is now streaming globally in five languages. If you missed it in theatres, this weekend is your chance.
body:
Here is a film that had no business being this good.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=aM5OLvxFBO4</youtube>

**Blast** — a Tamil martial arts action thriller about a middle-class family of karate practitioners who accidentally stumble into a ₹7,000-crore mining scam — was made for ₹18 crore. It grossed ₹69 crore worldwide in 19 days. And as of June 25, it's streaming on **Netflix** in Tamil, Hindi, Telugu, Kannada, and Malayalam, which means the Indian diaspora finally gets to see what all the noise was about.

The noise, it turns out, was entirely deserved.

## The Setup

Director **Subash K. Raj** — and this is his debut, which is almost offensive — built *Blast* around a deceptively simple premise. **Rajaram** (played by the veteran **Arjun Sarja**) is a karate master leading a quiet middle-class life. His wife **Neelaveni** (**Abhirami**) is equally skilled. Their daughter **Nila** (**Preity Mukhundhan**) works in IT by day and trains by night. They're not looking for trouble. They're a family that happens to be lethal.

Trouble finds them anyway, in the form of **Varun Dhayalan**, a ruthless corporate tycoon orchestrating a massive illegal mining operation. When the family crosses his path, what starts as a survival story turns into a full-blown takedown — corrupt authorities, deadly hitmen, corporate thugs. The Rajaram family doesn't call the police. They handle it themselves. With their fists.

## Why It Works

The genius of *Blast* is that it treats martial arts not as spectacle but as inheritance. This family fights the way other families cook together — it's communal, it's generational, it's intimate. The fight choreography, handled by **Phoenix Prabhu**, mixes raw street combat with disciplined technique, and the film gives each family member their own fighting style and their own moment to shine.

**Preity Mukhundhan** is the real revelation. Critics from *The Hindu* to *India Today* singled her out — she doesn't just perform the action sequences, she owns them. There's a moment in the second act where she goes from corporate professional to absolute hurricane, and the transition feels earned rather than scripted. This is her calling card, and she knows it.

The music is by **Ravi Basrur** — yes, the *KGF* man — and he brings that same rumbling, chest-thumping energy to a completely different kind of film. The cinematography by **Arun Radhakrishnan** gives the action sequences a gritty texture that feels more *The Raid* than typical Tamil masala.

Is the screenplay predictable in places? Sure. Is the runtime a little generous? *The Times of India* thought so. But as they also noted: debutant director Subash K. Raj knows exactly when enough is enough. The pacing never loses the audience, and the family dynamics ground everything in genuine emotion.

## The Numbers Don't Lie

Produced by **AGS Entertainment** on that ₹18-crore budget, *Blast* recouped its costs within the opening weekend. By day 19, it had cleared ₹47.58 crore nett in India and ₹68.75 crore worldwide — a certified blockbuster by any measure. For context, that's a return multiple that most ₹150-crore Bollywood productions would kill for.

This is the kind of film that reminds you why small-budget cinema, when it's done right, is more exciting than any franchise sequel. No IP recognition. No star power (with respect to Arjun Sarja's long career, this isn't a Rajinikanth opening). Just a good story, genuine skill, and the kind of action choreography that makes you sit forward in your seat.

## Where to Watch

Netflix, globally. Available in **Tamil** (original), **Hindi**, **Telugu**, **Kannada**, and **Malayalam**. If you're in the US, UK, or Canada and spent the last month reading about this film without being able to see it — your wait is over.

For diaspora families looking for a weekend watch that's both thrilling and surprisingly heartwarming, *Blast* is exactly the right call. It's a family film in the truest sense: a family that fights together, stays together. And punches really, really hard.
